mappings.note: Asks for metals by physical property (liquid at RT, knife-soft, best/worst heat conductor). Physical-property identification, so LO-1, not LO-2 -- no reactivity ordering is involved.
Defines malleability and ductility -- the physical properties LO-1 uses to classify metals. Nothing about reactivity or extraction.
Sodium is stored in kerosene because it is near the top of the reactivity series (reacts violently with air/moisture). Tests relative reactivity, so LO-2 rather than LO-1.
Equations for Fe/steam, Ca/water, K/water -- the graded water reactions that the reactivity series is built from. LO-2, not LO-1: the point is that the three differ in vigour.
Displacement table read to name the most reactive metal and arrange A-D in increasing reactivity. This is LO-2 verbatim.
Metal + dilute acid liberating hydrogen, and Fe + H2SO4. Displacement of hydrogen from acid is a reactivity-series behaviour, so LO-2 not LO-1.
Zn added to FeSO4 -- predicting a displacement reaction from relative position. LO-2.

Electron-dot structures and electron transfer forming Na2O/MgO. Ionic bond formation has no learning outcome in this frame; cited at the competency, which is explicitly about how compounds form from atomic structure and valency.

High melting point of ionic compounds follows from the lattice formed by electron transfer, so the C 1.1 competency. C 1.2 is about mixtures and separation techniques and does not cover ionic solids; no LO fits.
Minerals, ores and gangue are the vocabulary of extraction from ores -- LO-6. Not LO-7, which is corrosion and its prevention.
Metals found in the free (native) state -- occurrence, the first step of the extraction outcome LO-6.
Names the process that gets a metal out of its oxide (reduction) -- the core of LO-6.
Which metal/metal-oxide pairs displace, given the Mg > Zn > Cu activity order. Uses the reactivity series to predict displacement -- LO-2.
Which metals do not corrode easily -- corrosion resistance, LO-7. Not LO-2: no ordering or displacement prediction is asked for.
Definition of an alloy. Alloying appears in this frame only inside LO-7, so that is the nearest genuine slot even though the question does not mention corrosion.
Picks which of four metal/salt-solution pairs will displace. Straight LO-2.
Methods of preventing an iron pan from rusting (grease, paint, zinc coating) -- corrosion prevention, LO-7.
Deduces the element from the nature of its oxide (high melting point, water-soluble, therefore a basic metal oxide -> calcium). Classification from chemical properties, LO-1.
Tin rather than zinc on food cans because zinc is the more reactive metal. The graded answer is a reactivity comparison (LO-2), not the galvanisation mechanism of LO-7.

Designs a hammer/bulb-circuit test to separate metals from non-metals and then judges the test's usefulness. C 8.2-LO-2 is specifically about comparing the reactivity of TWO METALS, which this is not, so the competency C 8.2 carries the inquiry-design demand and LO-1 the content.
Amphoteric oxides and examples -- the nature of a metal oxide, used in LO-1 to classify elements by chemical property.
Metals that do and do not displace hydrogen from dilute acid -- position relative to hydrogen in the reactivity series, LO-2.
Anode, cathode and electrolyte in electrolytic refining. Refining is part of the extraction sequence in LO-6; no separate refining outcome exists.
Burning sulphur, gas on dry vs moist litmus, equation -- non-metal oxide is acidic. The oxide-nature test of LO-1.
Two ways to prevent rusting -- LO-7 exactly.
Type of oxide non-metals form with oxygen (acidic). Chemical-property classification, LO-1.

Four-part reason question: (a)(b)(c) turn on relative reactivity (noble metals, alkali metals under oil, aluminium's oxide layer) and (d) on roasting/calcination before reduction. Genuinely spans LO-2 and LO-6; part (c) also brushes LO-7 but corrosion prevention is not what is asked.
Sour juices clean tarnished copper because the acid dissolves the basic corrosion layer. Corrosion, LO-7, not the acid-metal reactivity of LO-2 -- the copper itself is not attacked.
Aqua regia dissolving gold bangles. The frame has no slot for aqua regia; its role in this chapter is that only it attacks the least reactive metals, so LO-2 is the nearest real outcome.
Copper, not steel, for hot-water tanks: steel would corrode. LO-7 rather than LO-2 because the failure being avoided is corrosion of the finished article.
Differentiates metals from non-metals on chemical properties (oxide nature, cation/anion formation, action with acids). LO-1's core demand.
Black coating on silver and green on copper -- names corrosion and its products. LO-7.
Identify Na, Mg and Cu using water alone. Content is the graded water reactivity (LO-2), and the task is to design a reactivity comparison with one reagent held fixed, which is C 8.2-LO-2.

Identifies iron from E2O3, resistance to water and the two chlorides ECl2/ECl3. The deciding evidence is variable valency, so the C 1.1 competency; no LO covers identifying which metal a set of compounds belongs to.
Oxide dissolves in HCl and turns red litmus blue, therefore basic, therefore a metal. Classification from chemical properties, LO-1.
Valence-shell count and the chloride formula for an element forming E2O. Valency-driven compound formation sits at the C 1.1 competency; neither LO covers writing formulae.

Sodium identified from the golden-yellow flame, then NaCl from a group-17 partner and NaOH by electrolysis. The chain is group position and compound formation, so C 1.1 rather than the reactivity-ordering LO-2.
Which property metals do not show (dullness). Physical-property classification, LO-1.
Malleability/ductility terminology. LO-1. (Stem is suspect -- see defect list: it says 'drawn into thin sheets' where the exemplar reads 'thin wires'.)
Which properties of aluminium suit cooking utensils (thermal conductivity, high melting point). Physical properties, LO-1.
Which metal reacts with neither cold nor hot water -- the water-reactivity gradient behind the series. LO-2.
Iron-plus-steam product on prolonged reaction (Fe3O4). A metal-water reaction, so LO-2; it is not corrosion in air, which would be LO-7.
Magnesium with water -- reacts less violently, hydrogen bubbles cling. Comparative vigour of a water reaction, LO-2.
Which acid fails to give hydrogen with metals (HNO3, an oxidising acid). The expectation being tested is the normal metal+acid hydrogen displacement of LO-2.

Aqua regia composition (3 conc HCl : 1 conc HNO3). No frame slot names aqua regia; it belongs to LO-2 as the reagent needed for metals at the bottom of the series. Cited at LO-2 rather than forced onto extraction.
Sorts ionic from covalent compounds (HCl, CCl4 are not ionic). Bond type from atomic structure -- the C 1.1 competency; no LO covers bonding.
Property ionic compounds do not show (conduction when solid). Same competency as the other ionic-property items; C 1.2 covers mixtures and separations, not ionic solids.
Which metals occur native (Au, Ag). Occurrence of low-reactivity metals, LO-6.
Which metals are electrolytically refined (Ag, Cu). Refining step of LO-6.
Silver blackens in air through Ag2S -- corrosion, LO-7.
Galvanisation is a zinc coating. LO-7 names galvanisation explicitly.
Stainless steel is iron with Ni and Cr -- alloying, which LO-7 names alongside galvanisation.
Green coating on copper is basic copper carbonate -- corrosion, LO-7.
Which metal is liquid at room temperature (Hg). Physical property, LO-1.
Na and Ca obtained by electrolysis of molten chlorides -- extraction of the most reactive metals, which LO-6 covers by naming low, medium and high reactivity.
The lustrous non-metal (iodine) -- an exception to the physical-property rule LO-1 is built on.
Which metal is displaced from its salt by the other three (Cu). Reactivity ordering used to predict displacement, LO-2.
Metal untouched by conc HCl and conc HNO3 separately but dissolved by the 3:1 mixture -> gold. Lowest-reactivity metal, LO-2, same reading as the other aqua regia items.
An alloy is a homogeneous mixture. Cited to LO-7, the only place alloying appears in this frame; the C 1.2 competency's 'types of mixtures' clause is about solutions and colloids, not alloys.
Electrolytic cell polarity (positive anode, negative cathode). Belongs to the electrolytic refining/reduction step of LO-6.
